en.title: Patricia Highsmith: The Monster Behind Mr. Ripley's Charm
en.summary: A new film shines a light on the later years of the acclaimed author, but was the creator of Tom Ripley truly as difficult as legend suggests? Those who knew her offer a complex portrait.
en.body:
The upcoming film exploring the later life of **Patricia Highsmith**, the celebrated author behind the chilling **Ripley** novels, invites a closer look at the woman who crafted such compelling tales of manipulation and suspense. While often remembered for her sharp, unsettling narratives, Highsmith herself was a figure of considerable complexity, inspiring a spectrum of reactions from those who encountered her.

Born in Texas in 1921 and later a long-term resident of Europe, Highsmith achieved international acclaim with her debut novel, **Strangers on a Train**, adapted by Alfred Hitchcock in 1951. Her most famous creation, Tom Ripley, first appeared in **The Talented Mr. Ripley** in 1970, a character whose amoral charm and ruthless ambition captivated readers and continues to inspire adaptations. Yet, behind the literary genius, Highsmith was described by many as a challenging personality. Publisher and bookseller **Otto Penzler** recalled an event at his New York shop where Highsmith, then 63, appeared taciturn and showed little patience for her few attendees, famously stating, "I can’t stand the bloody frogs" when Penzler attempted small talk about France.

> "She was a monster" — The Guardian Books

This perception of difficulty, however, is not universal. Her oldest friend, **Kate Skattebol**, remembered her as fun and possessing a great sense of humor in college, someone who "loved to shock people." British journalist **Francis Wyndham**, who met her in 1963, found her shy and reticent, but also sensed "deep feelings, someone who was affectionate but also difficult." Her American editor in the 1980s, **Gary Fisketjon**, also noted her complex nature. Some acquaintances and critics have labeled her a misogynist, while others argue for a broader misanthropy, suggesting her behavior might have been influenced by depression, alcoholism, or even Asperger syndrome. These conflicting accounts paint a picture not of a simple villain, but of a deeply private and often guarded individual.

## The Highsmith Enigma for Fans

For the legions of fans who devour **Highsmith**'s work, this duality is perhaps what makes her so fascinating. Her novels explore the darker aspects of human nature with an unflinching gaze, and understanding the author's own perceived eccentricities or difficulties adds another layer to the appreciation of her craft. The debate around her personality—whether she was a difficult recluse, a misunderstood genius, or something else entirely—fuels the ongoing intrigue surrounding her legacy. It’s this very tension between the polished, suspenseful narratives and the rumored abrasiveness of their creator that keeps readers returning to her chilling worlds, wondering about the mind that conceived them.

## What's Next

As new films and adaptations continue to bring **Patricia Highsmith**'s stories to wider audiences, her complex life and literary contributions remain fertile ground for discussion and analysis, ensuring her place as a master of psychological suspense.

content_raw: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”. Continue reading...
